title: Soil: what is in the mix?
subtitle: Spring 1 • Week 3 • Evidence lab
objective: Use evidence to show that soil contains rock material and organic matter.

sow.exactOutcome: Recognise that soils are made from rocks and organic matter.
sow.alignment: Direct match to C 30. Extends the required rock/organic distinction with air, water and evidence limits; no percentage composition is assumed.

priorLearning: Rocks are natural materials with different properties.
Living things grow; fallen leaves came from plants.
An observation is something we notice using a sense or a tool.
success: Identify one piece of mineral material and one piece of organic material.
Support a choice with something observed or stated on an evidence card.
Explain that soil is a mixture; air and water can occupy spaces between solids.

vocabulary.meaning: A mixture of mineral and organic material, with spaces for air and water.
Rock fragments and tiny mineral particles.
Material from living things, including broken-down remains.
A small space between soil particles.
Information that helps us decide whether an idea is supported.

equipment: Printed evidence cards and selected response page; pencils or highlighters.
Optional: teacher-screened soil in shallow lidded transparent trays, hand lenses, wooden sticks and spoons.
Optional teacher demonstration: clear plastic cup, small soil sample and room-temperature water.
preparation: Choose one pupil response route; all routes assess the same core science.
Print the six evidence cards and keep teacher answers separate.
For hands-on observation, screen samples for sharp objects, animal waste and heavy dust; use a known clean teaching source.
A second adult may pre-label two observable pieces. Do not depend on finding recognisable remains in every soil.
safety: No tasting, smelling closely or blowing soil; keep hands away from faces and wash hands afterwards.
Keep samples in trays and use tools; offer sealed-tray or paper observation to pupils avoiding touch.
Use plastic containers; an adult pours demonstration water slowly in a spill tray and wipes spills promptly.
Do not add living animals to the activity or collect unknown soil from contaminated sites.
practicalAlternative: Use the six printed evidence cards. Their described observations provide all information needed for every task. A bubble model substitutes for the optional demonstration; pupils label it as model evidence.

misconceptions.correction: Mineral material is one part; organic material is also present, and spaces can contain air and water.
misconceptions.check: Ask pupils to add a missing component to a rock-only model.

misconceptions.claim: Dark material must be organic matter.
misconceptions.correction: Colour alone does not identify what a particle is made from; dark minerals also exist.
misconceptions.check: Return to the dark-grain card and ask what else we need.

misconceptions.claim: Air is not part of soil because we cannot see it.
misconceptions.correction: Air can occupy pores. Escaping bubbles when water enters support that explanation.
misconceptions.check: Ask what occupied the spaces before the water.

misconceptions.claim: Mixing leaf pieces with sand makes fully developed soil at once.
misconceptions.correction: It makes a model mixture. Natural soils develop through interacting processes over time.
misconceptions.check: Ask which real processes the model leaves out.

access.supported: Read two cards aloud at a time. Pupil points, matches or dictates one evidence reason. Use the supported response page, with mineral/organic word bank.
access.standard: Classify evidence independently and write a two-part explanation that includes mineral and organic components.
access.stretch: Evaluate uncertain evidence and improve a rock-only model; explain one limit of the model.
access.regulation: Invite seated observation or paper evidence. Give predictable roles: observer, card mover, reporter. Reporting may be private; no timed competition or compulsory touching.

sources.title: USDA NRCS: Urban Soil Primer, chapter 2
sources.note: Checked 8 September 2026. Supports mineral material, organic matter, air and water as soil components and variation between soils. Teaching diagrams and evidence cards are original simplified models, not copied figures.

slides.title: Soil: what is in the mix?
body: What is hiding in a handful of soil?
slides.notes: Welcome pupils to a calm evidence lab. Accept initial ideas without confirming all. State the objective: use evidence to identify mineral and organic material. Choose handling or paper route privately.

slides.title: Start with what we know
body: 1. Did a fallen leaf come from a living thing?
2. Name one property of a rock.
3. What can a hand lens help us do?
slides.reveal: 1 Yes: a plant. 2 For example, hardness or colour. 3 See small details more clearly.
slides.notes: Read each question and allow spoken, pointed or written replies. Do not treat a quiet response as no understanding. If rock/material knowledge is insecure, point to A and name a mineral grain.

slides.title: Two sources, one mixture

visual.title: Two sources of soil material
visual.description: Rock weathering supplies mineral particles; living things supply organic material. These processes occur over time. Mixing this model does not instantly make mature soil.

slides.notes: Point to both branches. Think aloud: this rock breaks down and changes through weathering; it supplies mineral material. A fallen leaf came from a living plant. Its remains contribute organic matter. We are tracing sources, not saying every soil has equal amounts. Our mixed classroom model is not mature soil.

slides.title: Zoom into soil
body: Soil contains more than solid pieces.
Air and water fit into small spaces.

visual.title: A soil is a mixture
visual.description: Magnified model of soil: mineral grains, dead plant material, air spaces and water. The model does not show true sizes or fixed amounts.

elements.text: Model: sizes and amounts are not to scale.

slides.notes: Use the model, not a copied photo. Trace one mineral grain then a dead plant fragment. Point to one air pore and one water pore. State that real particles and pores differ greatly; this drawing does not give actual percentages or true sizes.

slides.title: A clue we cannot pick up

visual.title: What could the bubbles tell us?
visual.description: Before water is added, spaces between soil particles contain air. As water enters, some air escapes as bubbles. The drawing is a model, not a photograph or a measured result.

elements.text: Bubbles support: there was gas in the spaces.

slides.prompt: What was in the space first?
slides.reveal: Air was in some spaces. Water entering pushed some of it out.
slides.notes: Optional adult demonstration only; otherwise use this before/after model. Think aloud: I see bubbles, so there is gas. In this ordinary soil test, escaping air is a sensible explanation. The diagram is a model; it is not a record of our own experiment.

slides.title: The evidence desk
body: Read cards A, B and C.
Give one clue for each choice.

rows: Leaf vein; came from a fallen leaf
Fibres; came from a plant stem
table.caption: Constructed teaching evidence cards

slides.reveal: A: mineral. B and C: organic. Origin is stronger evidence than colour.
slides.notes: Pair roles: reader/observer and classifier, then swap. A: quartz identified as mineral, so mineral material. B/C: recognised plant remains, so organic. Invite a quiet pointing response plus adult-scribed reason. These are constructed examples, not observations made today.

slides.title: Accept, reject or need more?
body: F: a damp sample leaves a water mark.

rows: F supports water in the sample
table.caption: Use evidence cards D–F

slides.reveal: D: need more evidence. E and F: supported by the stated observations.
slides.notes: Give each pair three positions on paper: accept, reject, need more. The wording “D must be organic” overclaims; reject the certainty or choose need more, provided reasoning says colour cannot decide. E supports escaping air; F supports water. Press for “supports” rather than “proves everything about the sample”.

slides.title: Which account is best?
body: Choose one. Be ready to explain.

options.feedback: Mineral material is part of soil, but this misses organic material and pores.

options.text: Soil contains mineral and organic material; pores can contain air and water.
options.feedback: This includes the key solid components and the spaces between them.

options.text: Every dark speck is a dead plant.
options.feedback: Colour alone cannot tell us the material or its origin.

slides.notes: Require an individual choice before discussion. If many choose A, rebuild the two-branch diagram. If C, contrast a dark mineral with the leaf-vein evidence. If secure, invite “can contain” rather than claiming every pore always contains both air and water.

slides.title: Choose your evidence route
slides.notes: Give one route only, selected with the pupil. Supported uses A–C and the word bank; standard records all six cards; stretch assesses uncertain dark grains and improves a model. Pupils may observe screened soil too, but the evidence cards are sufficient.

slides.title: Look closely; keep a trace
body: Use cards or a screened sample.
Draw or name one thing you notice.
slides.notes: This slide shares the 12-minute You do stage. Hands-on: use a spoon or stick to move a small amount within a tray, observe with a lens, draw one mineral-looking grain and one identifiable plant fragment if present. Do not identify every tiny piece from appearance; record uncertain where appropriate. No sample is required for paper route.

slides.title: Build your explanation
body: Soil has mineral material such as __.
It has organic material such as __.
slides.prompt: What can you say with confidence?
slides.notes: Independent work time includes optional observation, route tasks and a brief check. Provide a spoken rehearsal before writing. Check that each pupil links evidence to a component, not only recites a word. Stretch pupils add air/water and a model limitation.

slides.title: Check your account
body: Have I named both kinds of material?
Have I kept an uncertain grain uncertain?
slides.notes: Shares the independent stage. Pupils use these checks to improve one response. Accept a private spoken improvement, a moved card, or a changed label as evidence of editing.

slides.title: Lundy loop: use your evidence
slides.prompt: Which part must we add to a rock-only model?
slides.reveal: Organic material; also show spaces for air and water.
slides.notes: Hear at least two different response routes without ranking them. Use one pupil suggestion to alter the drawn model and name the change. This gives the voice an actual influence. Ask one pupil to explain why the dark grain stayed uncertain.

slides.title: Three small checks
body: E3. What can fill a soil pore?
slides.reveal: A quartz grain; a leaf or stem fragment; air or water.
slides.notes: Collect exit page or three private spoken answers. Secure core: a mineral example and an organic example with sensible origins. If either is missing, start next lesson with A/B card matching. Air/water is extension to the core outcome, not a barrier to recording progress.

pupilPages.title: Evidence desk
pupilPages.intro: Constructed teaching examples. Cut cards or point to them. Use these even if no soil is available.

cards.title: A • Pale grain
cards.text: Under a hand lens: a hard, gritty quartz grain. Quartz is a mineral found in rocks.

cards.title: B • Leaf piece
cards.text: A soft brown fragment with a clear leaf vein. It came from a fallen leaf.

cards.title: C • Tiny stem
cards.text: A short woody piece with visible fibres. It came from a plant stem.

cards.title: D • Dark grain
cards.text: A dark speck. Its colour is visible, but its material is not identified.

cards.title: E • Bubbles
cards.text: When water is poured onto this soil, bubbles rise from spaces between particles.

cards.title: F • Water
cards.text: A damp sample leaves a water mark on absorbent paper. No liquid was added during this observation.

blocks.prompt: W1. Sort A, B and C. Give one evidence clue.
W2. Which of D–F needs more evidence? Why?

pupilPages.title: Route 1 • Match and explain
pupilPages.intro: Choose this route for supported recording. An adult may read or scribe your words.

blocks.prompt: S1. A is a quartz grain. Choose its group.
S2. B is a fallen-leaf piece. Choose its group.
S3. Use a clue: I put C with organic matter because __.
S4. Soil is a mixture of __ and __. Word bank: mineral material / organic matter.
S5. Draw or name a soil pore. What might be in it?

pupilPages.title: Route 2 • Write an evidence record
pupilPages.intro: Use cards A–F. Record only what the evidence supports.

blocks.prompt: T2. Explain why soil is more than broken rock.
T3. A classmate says “D is organic because it is dark.” What would you say?

pupilPages.title: Route 3 • Improve the model
pupilPages.intro: A designer draws soil as tightly packed grey stones, with no gaps.

blocks.prompt: X1. Sketch a better model. Label mineral material, organic matter and one pore.
X2. Add air or water. Explain where you put it.
X3. Why can the dark-grain card not decide its material?
X4. What can your model help explain? What does it leave out?

pupilPages.title: Exit and reflection
pupilPages.intro: Complete the three exit checks. You may point, draw, write or tell an adult.

blocks.prompt: E1. Name or draw one mineral example from today.
E2. Name or draw one organic example from today.
E3. What can fill a soil pore?
R1. One idea I changed after hearing evidence was __.
R2. Next time, I would like to observe or ask __.

answers.label: Retrieval 1–3
answers.answer: 1 Yes, a fallen leaf came from a living plant. 2 Accept hardness, colour, texture or another suitable property; not “all rocks are heavy/hard”. 3 A lens magnifies small visible details.

answers.label: We do W1 / cards A–C
answers.answer: A mineral: quartz is identified as a mineral from rocks. B organic: recognised fallen-leaf tissue/vein. C organic: plant-stem fibres. Colour is not the deciding clue.

answers.label: We do W2 / cards D–F
answers.answer: D remains uncertain; dark colour alone is insufficient. E supports air/gas occupying pores before water displaced it. F supports water in that damp sample. Neither E nor F tells us the percentages of each component.

answers.label: Hinge
answers.answer: Second option is correct. Rock-only misses organic matter and pore contents. Dark colour does not show every grain is a dead plant. Reteach with the two-source diagram and cards A/B if needed.

answers.label: S1–S5
answers.answer: S1 mineral material. S2 organic matter. S3 it came from a plant stem / has recognisable plant fibres. S4 mineral material and organic matter. S5 a space between particles containing air or water; accept a labelled sketch.

answers.label: T1
answers.answer: A mineral—quartz origin. B organic—leaf vein/plant origin. C organic—stem/fibres. D uncertain—only colour known. E air in spaces—bubbles escape as water enters. F water—damp sample leaves water mark.

answers.label: T2–T3
answers.answer: T2 soil also contains organic matter from living things and pores that can contain air/water. Core credit requires organic matter alongside mineral material. T3 colour is not sufficient; we need information about its material/origin or further examination. Do not demand an unavailable laboratory test name.

answers.label: X1–X4
answers.answer: X1 include mineral grains and organic fragments, with labelled gaps. X2 air/water goes in gaps, not inside every solid particle. X3 dark minerals and organic pieces can both be dark. X4 model helps explain a mixture or pore spaces; it does not show actual sizes, proportions, organisms, chemistry or long formation processes. Accept any accurate limitation.

answers.label: Exit E1–E3
answers.answer: E1 quartz grain, rock fragment or mineral particle. E2 leaf/stem remains or another valid example. E3 air or water. Do not demand both if the prompt is singular.

answers.label: R1–R2
answers.answer: Reflective answers vary. Accept an evidence-related revision, e.g. “I thought soil was only rock; leaf fibres changed my mind.” R2 should be a relevant question or observation; no fixed right preference.

answers.label: Optional observation
answers.answer: Actual results vary. Record visible observations without inventing identifiable organic fragments. “Cannot tell” is scientifically valid for an unidentifiable particle; pair it with card evidence so the core objective can still be assessed.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2; retrieval 3; I do 7; We do 8; hinge 3; You do 12; review 3; exit 2. Zero-minute slides share the stage time.
The BUILD SoW uses a Year 3 science anchor presented age-appropriately for older learners. These are access routes, not diagnoses or permanent attainment groups.

Teach the word organic in its science meaning here: material from living things, not a supermarket production label. Living organisms also inhabit soil; visible leaf fragments are not all of its organic matter.
A cover teacher can teach every task with paper cards. Say: “We will use the evidence we have. If it does not decide, we will say uncertain.”
Assess reasoning through a pointing choice plus spoken clue as readily as extended writing. No public ranking. Secure core is identifying mineral and organic components with a relevant example.
The three-lesson sequence moves from composition to comparative drainage to an estimated water balance. Keep the distinction between looking, testing and claiming clear.
